title: New pornography offences in the UK
subtitle: What Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 actually criminalises, where it applies, and where the participant defences leave a gap.
summary: From 6 November 2026, England and Wales has three new offences of possessing or publishing certain pornographic images: strangulation or suffocation; penetrative sex between people a reasonable person would think are, or are pretending to be, related; and sexual activity where a reasonable person would think at least one person is, or is pretending to be, under 16. A Scottish strangulation offence remains prospective and, once in force, will be stricter. The new offences largely target third-party possession and publication beyond the participants. This page sets out the statutory text, commencement and extent, and then tests two edge cases in a labelled “cheeky table”. It is legal research, not legal advice, and it is not a guide to producing any image.
scope: United Kingdom, with the territorial differences set out below. Sections 104, 106 and 107 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 are in force in England and Wales from 6 November 2026. Section 104 also extends to Northern Ireland but has not been commenced there. Section 105, for Scotland, is not in force. If an image depicts a person who is actually under 18, the Protection of Children Act 1978, section 160 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and related offences apply in addition to anything on this page.
status_note: The statutes and commencement instruments cited were read from legislation.gov.uk on 23 November 2026. The CPS Obscene Publications guidance was read the same day. All five commencement instruments made under the 2026 Act up to Commencement No. 5 were checked for the semen-defaced-image offence. Items marked as our analysis are our interpretation, not findings of a court. This is legal research and commentary, not legal advice.

highlights.label: In force
highlights.detail: Sections 104, 106 and 107 are in force in England and Wales. The Scottish strangulation offence remains prospective.

highlights.label: The recording gap
highlights.detail: For some role-play cases the new offences do not ban a participant’s private recording. They ban possession by others, and publication beyond the participants.

highlights.label: Scotland
highlights.detail: Once section 105 is in force, a recording of real strangulation has no participant defence in Scotland, even if the act was consensual and caused no injury.

highlights.label: Section 98
highlights.detail: The enacted offence of sharing a semen-defaced image has not been commenced. Only a related Online Safety Act amendment was brought in on 29 June 2026.

sections.title: The new offences
sections.intro: Four sections in Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 add new possession and publication offences for certain pornographic images. They sit alongside the older extreme-pornography offence, not in place of it.

paragraphs.text: Section 104 inserts sections 67A to 67D into the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008. It is an offence to possess or publish a pornographic image that portrays, in an explicit and realistic way, a person strangling or suffocating another person, where a reasonable person looking at the image would think that the persons were real. Publishing includes giving or making the image available to another person by any means.

Section 106 inserts sections 67E to 67G. The image must be pornographic and must portray, in an explicit and realistic way, sexual penetration of the vagina or anus with a body part or anything else, or of the mouth by a penis. A reasonable person must think the people were real, and — taking into account any sound or information associated with the image — that they were related, or pretending to be related, in a listed way. For blood and adoptive relationships the offence is not limited by age. For step and foster relationships, at least one person must be, or be pretending to be, under 18. A fanciful pretence of relationship is excluded.

Section 107 inserts sections 67H to 67J. Possession or publication is an offence where a reasonable person, looking at a pornographic image and taking into account any associated sound or information, would think that it portrays, in an explicit and realistic way, sexual activity between two people who are real, and that at least one of them is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Penetration is not required. A person is not to be taken as pretending to be under 16 if it is fanciful that they actually are under 16 in the way pretended.

If anyone depicted is actually under 18, other offences already apply, including taking, making or distributing an indecent photograph of a child and possession of such a photograph. Section 107 does not replace those offences. The participant defence to section 107 is unavailable if either person was in fact under 16. This page discusses the new imagery offences, including the statutory treatment of adult role-play. It is not a guide to producing any image, and it does not discuss, and is not about, sexual images of actual children.

Section 105 would insert sections 51D to 51G into the Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982, creating a Scottish offence of possessing or publishing pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation. It is not in force.

Sections 104(1) to (3) came into force on 6 November 2026 so far as they extend to England and Wales. Sections 106 and 107 came into force on the same day. These dates are set by regulation 2 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 (Commencement No. 4) Regulations 2026. Section 105 has not been commenced.

links.text: regulation 2 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 (Commencement No. 4) Regulations 2026

paragraphs.text: On conviction on indictment in England and Wales, possession under section 67A or 67E carries a maximum of two years, and possession under section 67H a maximum of three years. Publication of any of those images carries a maximum of five years. Proceedings in England and Wales may not be instituted except by or with the consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions. For the section 104 offence in Northern Ireland, once commenced, the consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland would be required.

The same indictment maxima are written into the Scottish section 105 offence: two years for possession and five years for publication, once that section is in force. A claim that the Scottish possession maximum is three years is not supported by the enacted text.

sections.title: Sources and legislation
sections.intro: The claims on this page are taken from the official text, and from Crown Prosecution Service guidance and contemporaneous reporting where that is stated. Each link goes to the source cited.

paragraphs.text: Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 is the pornography chapter. The individual offence-creating sections are 104, 105, 106 and 107. Extent is set out in section 254. Section 98 and Schedule 13 deal with semen-defaced images and related intimate-image amendments. Section 99 inserts a separate offence of making or supplying a purported intimate image generator. Section 113, in force from 29 September 2026, restates the exposure offence in section 66 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003.

links.text: Part 5, Chapter 4 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026

paragraphs.text: Commencement of the pornography offences is in the Commencement No. 4 Regulations. Commencement of section 98, so far as it has been commenced at all, and of section 99, is in the Commencement No. 1 Regulations. We also read Commencement No. 2, No. 3 and No. 5 to check whether the semen-defaced-image offence had been brought into force later. It had not, as at 23 November 2026.

entries.title: The older statutes these offences sit with

paragraphs.text: The new offences use the definition of a “pornographic” image in section 63 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, and they use the definition of “non-consensual harm” in section 66(3) of that Act. Section 63 remains the extreme-pornography possession offence. Section 75A of the Serious Crime Act 2015 is the offline offence of strangulation or suffocation in England and Wales. Sections 64 and 65 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 criminalise penetrative sex between listed adult blood and adoptive relatives. Section 66 of that Act is the exposure offence. Section 66B covers sharing, or threatening to share, an intimate photograph or film. Section 66E, inserted by section 138 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and in force from 6 February 2026, is the offence of creating a purported intimate image of an adult.

links.text: section 63 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008
Section 75A of the Serious Crime Act 2015
Sections 64 and 65 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003

paragraphs.text: Section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 is the offence of possessing a prohibited non-photographic image of a child. Section 65 of that Act defines “image” and “child”, including imaginary children and the “impression conveyed” test. The Obscene Publications Act 1959, section 2, criminalises publication of an obscene article, and having an obscene article for publication for gain is covered by the 1964 Act. Private possession, without publication or an intention to publish for gain, is not an offence under those Acts.

links.text: Section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009

paragraphs.text: The Crown Prosecution Service Obscene Publications guidance, as read on 23 November 2026, already lists the new 6 November 2026 offences. On the 1959 Act itself, the guidance says that content relating to non-criminal conduct is unlikely to be obscene provided the audience is not young or otherwise vulnerable, and that a prosecution under the Act is not likely where the conduct is consensual, no serious harm is caused, the conduct is not inextricably linked with other criminality, and the likely audience is not under 18 or otherwise vulnerable.

links.text: Crown Prosecution Service Obscene Publications guidance

paragraphs.text: On 6 January 2012 a jury at Southwark Crown Court acquitted Michael Peacock of six charges under the Obscene Publications Act arising from the sale of DVDs to an undercover officer. BBC News and The Guardian reported the unanimous not guilty verdicts. The Guardian reported that the material included so-called “water-sports” and other acts that are legal between consenting adults. The films themselves were not independently reviewed for this page.

sections.title: Our analysis
sections.intro: The notes below follow the structure of the supplied analysis, checked against the primary text. Where that draft overstated or mis-cited the law, the corrected position is set out here. This is our commentary, not legal advice.

entries.title: Extent, and what is actually in force
entries.kind: Our analysis of the statute and commencement regulations

paragraphs.text: The default extent of the 2026 Act is England and Wales only. Section 104(1) to (3) — the strangulation offence itself and the associated information-society-service rules — extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland. Section 104(5), the Online Safety Act amendment, extends to the whole United Kingdom. Sections 106(2) and (3) and 107(2) and (3), certain ancillary provisions, extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland. Sections 106(7) and 107(5), the Online Safety Act amendments, extend to the whole United Kingdom. The offence-creating subsections of sections 106 and 107 themselves follow the default and extend to England and Wales only. Section 105 extends to Scotland only.

Extent is not the same as commencement. Regulation 2(a) of the Commencement No. 4 Regulations brought section 104(1) to (3) into force on 6 November 2026 only “so far as it extends to England and Wales”. The Northern Ireland extent of that offence has not been commenced. Sections 106 and 107 were commenced in full on the same day, but the offences themselves only extend to England and Wales.

The participant defences in the new England and Wales offences — sections 67B, 67F and 67I — use the existing definition in section 66(3) of the 2008 Act. Harm inflicted on a person is “non-consensual” harm if (a) the harm is of such a nature that the person cannot, in law, consent to it being inflicted on himself or herself; or (b) where the person can, in law, consent to it being so inflicted, the person does not in fact consent to it being so inflicted. Those are the two limbs of section 66(3), now verified from the official text.

For strangulation imagery in England and Wales, the participant defence therefore fails if the act involved harm that the law does not allow a person to consent to, or harm to which the person did not in fact consent. That is our reading of the cross-reference, not a judicial determination of any particular image or injury.

Section 75A of the Serious Crime Act 2015 makes it an offence in England and Wales intentionally to strangle another person, or to do any other act that affects the person’s ability to breathe and constitutes battery. Consent is a defence, but that defence does not apply if the person suffers “serious harm” and the defendant intended that harm or was reckless as to it. “Serious harm” is defined as grievous bodily harm, wounding, or actual bodily harm. The consent defence is evidential: sufficient evidence must be adduced to raise the issue, and the prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt.

This is the offline statutory baseline that the England and Wales pornography participant defence appears designed to track. The two tests are not worded identically. Whether a given injury that would defeat the section 75A consent defence also amounts to “non-consensual harm” under section 66(3) would be a question for a court. That last sentence is our analysis.

entries.title: Scotland compared with England and Wales

paragraphs.text: In England and Wales, the section 67B participant defence is available if the person directly participated in the act portrayed and the act did not involve the infliction of any non-consensual harm on any person. For publication, the image must also have been published only to other people who directly participated.

The Scottish defence, once section 105 is in force, is available only if the person directly participated and “the act did not actually involve strangulation or suffocation of any person”. For publication, the image must also have been published only to other participants. The wording is in the 2026 Act itself, as the text that will be inserted as sections 51D to 51G of the Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982.

The Scottish version is stricter. A recording of real strangulation would have no participant defence in Scotland, even if the act was fully consensual and caused no injury. England and Wales allows the defence provided the harm threshold in section 66 is not crossed. That comparison is our analysis of the enacted wording. Section 105 is still prospective.

The statutory heading is “Pornographic images of sexual activity with child under 16”. The elements, confirmed from the inserted section 67H, are these. The image must be pornographic. A reasonable person, looking at it and taking into account any associated sound or information, must think that it portrays, in an explicit and realistic way, sexual activity between two people; that those people are real; and that at least one of them is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Penetration is not required. A fanciful pretence of being under 16 is excluded. The participant defence requires direct participation, no non-consensual harm, and that neither person was actually under 16. For the publication offence, the image must also have been published only to the other participant. The indictment maxima are three years for possession and five years for publication. The Director of Public Prosecutions must consent to proceedings.

Those elements include adult role-play imagery. They also include imagery of a person who is actually under 16. In that second case the participant defence is unavailable, and the Protection of Children Act 1978 and section 160 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 are the primary offences. Nothing on this page should be read as commenting on, or offering any analysis of how to produce, sexual images of actual children.

paragraphs.text: The table is our analysis of how the new offences and the participant defences apply to typical scenarios. It is not a statement that any scenario is lawful for all purposes. Other offences — including those protecting children, the extreme-pornography offence, the Obscene Publications Act, and public-order or public-decency offences — may still apply on particular facts.

The new offences largely do not criminalise the private recording, by the participants themselves, of an act that was lawful to perform, subject to the non-consensual-harm limit in England and Wales and to the “no actual strangulation” limit in Scotland once section 105 is in force. They criminalise possession by third parties and publication beyond the participants. That is the “lawful to do, lawful to record and keep, criminal to share” gap in the role-play cases.

For actual blood or adoptive relatives in a listed relationship, that gap does not exist. The offline penetrative act is already an offence under sections 64 and 65 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003, and the participant defence to the imagery offence is unavailable.

AI-generated images can be caught by the new offences, and by section 63, if the relevant reasonable-person tests are satisfied. Each of those offences requires that a reasonable person looking at the image would think the people were real. For section 107, that assessment also takes into account associated sound or information.

Possession is, in principle, a continuing act. An image still held after 6 November 2026 can be possessed on or after the commencement date even if it was first acquired earlier. That is our analysis of the ordinary meaning of a possession offence. We found no transitional exemption in the Commencement No. 4 Regulations, and no official guidance on cloud backups, caches or shared accounts. That last point remains unverified.

paragraphs.text: These corrections are taken from the official text of the Act, the five commencement instruments, the current CPS guidance, and the Sexual Offences Act and Data (Use and Access) Act provisions cited above. A further claim, that the BBFC still refuses R18 certificates for certain fluid acts on physical discs, was not independently verified against the current classification guidelines and is not relied on below.

Three items in the supplied analysis can now be closed. The wording of the Scottish sections 51D to 51G is in section 105 of the 2026 Act and is set out above, though those sections have not yet been inserted because section 105 is not in force. The two limbs of section 66(3) of the 2008 Act have been read from the official text. The section 75A consent rules have been read from the official text.

These points remain unverified. We found no CPS or official guidance on whether, or how, the new possession offences apply to cloud backups, caches or shared accounts, or on the continuing-possession point more generally. We have not independently verified current BBFC R18 practice on depictions of bodily fluids. We have not attempted to confirm historical Hansard column or amendment numbers, which the source notes already treated as unconfirmed.

sections.intro: Two edge cases, taken from the supplied notes, tested against the statutes cited above. The conclusions are our analysis of scope, not a prediction of any charging decision or verdict.

paragraphs.text: We do not suggest, we do not advocate, we do not support, we do not find enjoyable in any way, shape or form. The point of the “cheeky table” is to analyse and fine-tune the existing gaps that were left there on purpose. Or maybe by accident? Anyway, that’s the law. Talking about the law should not be an offence.

entries.title: Consenting adults, private premises, no penetration

paragraphs.text: On the face of the statutes, neither the new Chapter 4 offences nor the extreme-pornography offence criminalises consenting adults, in private, engaging in mutual masturbation or in activity involving bodily fluids, including semen or urine, where no listed act is portrayed.

Sections 104 and 107 are not engaged if there is no strangulation or suffocation, and no portrayal of a person who is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Section 106 is not engaged by mutual masturbation even if the people were framed as biological siblings, because section 67E requires sexual penetration of the vagina or anus, or of the mouth by a penis.

Section 63 of the 2008 Act is a closed list. Subsection (7) covers acts that threaten life; acts that result, or are likely to result, in serious injury to a person’s anus, breasts or genitals; sexual interference with a human corpse; and intercourse or oral sex with an animal. Subsection (7A), added later, covers two forms of non-consensual penetration. In each case a reasonable person looking at the image must think the people, or the person or animal, were real, and the image must also be grossly offensive, disgusting or otherwise of an obscene character. Bodily fluids are not a listed category.

Private possession is not an offence under the Obscene Publications Act 1959. The 1959 Act, as read with the 1964 Act, covers publication, and having an obscene article for publication for gain. On publication, the current CPS guidance does not list particular sexual acts. It says a prosecution under the Act is not likely where the conduct is consensual, no serious harm is caused, the conduct is not inextricably linked with other criminality, and the likely audience is not under 18 or otherwise vulnerable. The 2012 acquittal in R v Peacock is consistent with that approach, but it does not make such prosecutions “obsolete”. Whether any given publication would be charged remains a fact-specific decision.

entries.title: Two traps to watch, one of them not yet in force

paragraphs.text: Schedule 13, paragraph 2 of the 2026 Act would insert a new section 66AA into the Sexual Offences Act 2003, “Sharing semen-defaced image”. A person would commit an offence by intentionally sharing a semen-defaced image of another person, without that person’s consent, and without a reasonable belief in consent. A “semen-defaced image” is a photograph or film which shows, or appears to show, that person and which has, or appears to have, semen on it or in its immediate vicinity, or a photograph or film of such an image. The offence is the sharing, not the private act between consenting participants. There is a reasonable-excuse defence, and an exception where the image had already been publicly shared with consent. It would be a summary-only offence. As at 23 November 2026 this provision remains prospective. It should not be described as already in force.

Venue is a different issue. Section 66 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 is the offence of “Exposure”. From 29 September 2026, a person who intentionally exposes their genitals commits the offence if they intend that someone will see the genitals and be caused alarm, distress or humiliation, or if they expose them for sexual gratification with the intention that someone will see them and being reckless as to whether someone who sees them will be caused alarm, distress or humiliation. That is not automatic merely because the setting is a public swimming pool; the mental elements have to be proved. Common-law outraging public decency is a separate offence, and other public-place legislation may also arise on particular facts.

entries.title: An AI-generated fictional adult with additional breasts

paragraphs.text: The supplied notes treat an AI-generated erotic image of a fictional adult with four breasts as falling outside the 2008 and 2026 pornography offences. Two points in the statutes are relevant. First, section 63 and the new Chapter 4 offences all require that a reasonable person looking at the image would think the person, or persons, were real. Second, even if that test were met, four breasts, without more, are not a listed act under section 63, section 67A, section 67E or section 67H.

Whether a particular image would fail the “real person” test is a question of fact, not a rule of law. It can be argued that a torso with four breasts would not be taken by a reasonable person as a real human being. A prosecutor might invite a different conclusion by reference to rare congenital conditions. We do not treat the “real person” filter as an automatic defence, and we do not describe the scenario as “completely lawful” or “double-insulated”. On the face of the listed-act requirements, additional breasts alone do not supply the underlying offence.

First, section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 — possession of a prohibited image of a child — is a different regime. It applies to non-photographic images, including computer-generated images, and it has no “reasonable person would think the person was real” requirement of the kind found in section 63 and in Chapter 4. A “child” is a person under 18. References to an image of a child include an imaginary child. Where an image shows a person, it is to be treated as an image of a child if the impression conveyed is that the person shown is a child, or if that is the predominant impression even though some of the physical characteristics shown are not those of a child. Fantasy anatomy does not, by itself, take an image outside section 62 if the character is depicted as under 18. The image must still be pornographic, fall within the listed forms of content, and be grossly offensive, disgusting or otherwise of an obscene character.

Second, creating or sharing a purported intimate image of a real, identifiable person without consent is already a crime, whether or not the image also alters the person’s anatomy. The creating offence is section 66E of the Sexual Offences Act 2003, inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and in force from 6 February 2026. Sharing an image that shows, or appears to show, another person in an intimate state can engage section 66B. Section 99 of the 2026 Act, in force from 29 June 2026, is not that offence. It inserts section 66I, which criminalises making or supplying a thing for use as a generator of purported intimate images.

Third, if a generated image passed the “appears real” test and also portrayed a listed extreme act — for example an act involving a human corpse, an animal, or non-consensual penetration — section 63 would be capable of applying to that act. The additional breasts would not be what made the image extreme.
